title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch took leave of Betsy in the drawing-room and went in to his wife. She was lying down, but hearing his steps she sat up quickly into her earlier posture and looked at him in alarm. He saw she had been crying.

"I'm very grateful for your trust in me." He repeated gently in Russian the phrase he had said in French in front of Betsy, and sat down beside her. When he spoke to her in Russian, using the intimate, affectionate "thou," it was unbearably irritating to Anna. "And I'm very grateful for your decision. I too think that since he is leaving, there's no need at all for Count Vronsky to come here. However, if...."

"But I've already said so, so why repeat it?" Anna suddenly interrupted, unable to suppress her irritation. "No need at all," she thought, "for a man to come and say good-bye to the woman he loves, the woman he was ready to ruin himself for, and has ruined himself for, and who can't live without him. No need at all!" She compressed her lips, and dropped her burning eyes to his hands with their swollen veins. They were rubbing each other.
"Let's never speak of it," she added more calmly.
"I've left this question to you to decide, and I am very glad to see...." Alexey Alexandrovitch was beginning.
"That my wish coincides with your own," she finished quickly, exasperated at his speaking so slowly when she already knew everything he was going to say.
"Yes," he agreed; "and Princess Tverskaya's interference in such difficult private matters is entirely uncalled for. She, of all people...."
"I don't believe a word of what's said about her," Anna said quickly. "I know she truly cares about me."

Alexey Alexandrovitch sighed and said nothing. She fingered the tassel of her dressing-gown nervously, glancing at him with that torturing sense of physical revulsion for which she blamed herself but couldn't control. Her only wish now was to be free of his oppressive presence.
"I've just sent for the doctor," said Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"I'm perfectly well — what do I want the doctor for?"
"No, the little one is crying, and they say the nurse hasn't enough milk."

"Why didn't you let me nurse her, when I begged to? Anyway" (Alexey Alexandrovitch understood what was meant by that "anyway"), "she's a baby, and they're killing her." She rang the bell and ordered the baby brought to her. "I begged to nurse her, I wasn't allowed to, and now I'm blamed for it."
"Yes you are blaming me! My God! Why didn't I die!" And she burst into sobs. "Forgive me, I'm on edge, I'm being unjust," she said, controlling herself, "but please, go away...."
"No, this can't go on," Alexey Alexandrovitch said to himself firmly as he left his wife's room.

Never before had the impossibility of his position in the eyes of the world, and his wife's hatred of him, and the whole weight of that mysterious brutal force that guided his life against his spiritual inclinations and demanded conformity with its decrees and a change in his attitude toward his wife — never had all of this been laid before him as plainly as it was that day. He saw clearly that the whole world and his wife expected something from him, but what exactly, he couldn't make out. He felt this was stirring up in him an anger that was destroying his peace of mind and all the good of what he had attained. He believed it would be better for Anna herself to break off all relations with Vronsky; but if everyone considered that out of the question, he was even ready to let those relations be renewed, as long as the children weren't disgraced, as long as he wasn't deprived of them or forced to change his position. As bad as that would be, it was still better than a rupture, which would put her in a hopeless and shameful position and strip him of everything he cared about. But he felt helpless; he knew in advance that everyone was against him, and that he wouldn't be allowed to do what now seemed to him so natural and right, but would be forced to do what was wrong, though it seemed to them the proper thing.
